newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya bond issue flops, blamed on poor marketing.
newsitem.headline: Kenya bond issue flops, blamed on poor marketing.

text.p: A weak and uncoordinated marketing effort by the Central Bank of Kenya was blamed on Tuesday for the low sales of the bank's first floating-rate treasury bond this month.
Brokers at the Nairobi Stock Exchange said the bank's approach to the first issue, worth $93 million, had led to a dismal response by the public at auction.

"They've basically handled this issue like it is a wholesale product not realising that because of its retail nature they need to use other players in the market who have access to the type of investors they're targeting," one broker said.
The bank offered the floating rate bond to attract small investors, giving them an alternative to treasury bills whose returns are comparable.

The bond has a minimum investment amount of 50,000 shillings and is pegged to the 91-day treasury bill, for which the minimum investment has been raised to one million shillings. The 91-day T-bill has a current average yield of 21.655 percent.
For a total of five billion shillings of bonds offered to the public, the bank received 77 bids totalling only 260 million shillings. It accepted some 63 bids totalling 17.61 million shillings.

Brokers said the bank could have made the issue an immediate success. "For one, they said they would trade them on the floor, and secondly they should have at least appointed a registrar and a receiving bank," a senior broker told Reuters.
No senior official at the central bank was available for comment on Monday and Tuesday.
The bank announced last week, after the poor response at the auction, that it would begin trading the bonds in March at the Nairobi bourse.
Robert Mathu, business development manager at the bourse, said the bank had not yet lodged an official application for listing at the stock exchange.

"But we're currently working on modalities. In particular, the issue of a registrar needs to be addressed so that there will be no hitches in the transfer process once a transaction is completed," he added.
Financial analysts said there was no reason why the bank's bonds should not perform as well any other bond given the fact that they are issued by the central bank, a reliable guarantor.
"It looks like it is more of a technical problem -- wrong timing and a definite lack of information about the product," one said.

They added it was still too early to draw any final conclusions. "It is still in the transition stage, shifting from selling directly to the public. The bank will now have to work closely with professional intermediaries especially brokers because they are involved a lot in direct investment advice," one analyst said.
"Bonds can do well in our market because they are very liquid but people need to know about them," a senior broker said.
The bank has invited applications for the floating-rate treasury bond for the next auction to be held on January 30. ($=54.78 shillings
